title: Anthropic's AI Safety Bill Targets Small Labs with Outdated 10^25 FLOPs Bar
summary:
Industry critics argue that Anthropic is trying to protect its market position by including specific technical benchmarks in a draft safety bill that would over-regulate smaller competitors. The bill defines the regulatory frontier using a 10²⁵ FLOPs threshold, which figures like David Sacks claim is a stale 2023 EU standard that targets startups while exempting modern frontier models like GPT-6 Astra trained on 10²⁷ FLOPs. In response, federal affairs lead AJ Cimino stated the draft is a translation of the company's Advanced AI Framework and confirmed that Anthropic plans to update the language regarding state-level preemption to better preserve state authority.

Safety advocates and figures such as Gary Marcus have slammed the proposal's high bar for government intervention, which requires a foreseeable risk of $1 billion in damages or more than 50 deaths or serious injuries to block a model. Critics argue these limits, alongside the requirement for judicial approval, disempower the Commerce Department's ability to stop dangerous releases. Anthropic defends these thresholds as necessary safeguards against the capricious use of government power, though Cimino noted the company is re-evaluating the limits to ensure a strong national standard.

I think this (Politico leaking a bad federal bill Anthropic has been pitching) is a really important moment to call on Anthropic to act like it means it:

a) It’s nakedly self-interested for Anthropic to shop around provisions that serve to protect its own wiggle room and its own ability to adjudicate internal and external deployment decisions on Slack (while also publicly warning that its AI might end the world). USG should retain more emergency optionality without having to make an unreasonably detailed affirmative case that predicts whether 50 people will die or 49.

b) I get that Anthropic is worried about model blocking authority being used capriciously. I am too. And maybe this is more about Anthropic’s general distrust of the current admin. Then why preempt states so broadly at the same time? Shouldn’t you *want* California to pass a law that clarifies how and when emergency injunction authority will be used there, and designates it to an expert-staffed authority whose final calls are not arbitrary, but informed by independent embedded evaluators? Shouldn’t you *want* to have more purpose-built tools in our arsenal and not just sledgehammers and export controls?

c) Let’s say this has nothing to do with self-interest at all and reflects a genuinely held belief that it’s time to phase out state-led AI regulation and put Congress in charge, based on some idealized view of what different government actors should and shouldn’t do. I too would love for Congress to pass a strong law that establishes a federal regulator! But given that Congress is still the same dysfunctional Congress it always was, I think the premature preemption view is absurd taken with what Anthropic execs believe about how fast things are moving and how high the stakes are. And it’s definitely absurd taken with the fact that Anthropic is doing plenty of things it wouldn’t do in an ideal world (e.g. racing full steam ahead to RSI), and seems content to ride on its realpolitik estimations of the current landscape of actors there.

Anthropic needs to do better going forward.

@_NathanCalvin I lead our federal affairs team at @AnthropicAI and wanted to share a few thoughts on the draft federal AI safety bill text that's been circulating this weekend after a version was shared with the press.

First, some process. We’ve been advocating for the concepts in our Advanced AI Framework [https://t.co/oouadYKyVs] proposal for months. Understandably, federal policymakers wanted to know what this could look like in bill form. This draft is a translation of those ideas into legislative language, shared with a small number of congressional offices that have been working on these issues. It doesn’t include everything we would ultimately like to see passed into law. In part because some ideas (like those shared in Dario’s essay on pacing [​​https://t.co/7ZvRZhLqFO] a few weeks ago) are so new that we are still working on if or how they can be converted into policy language.

It is worth saying where we stand on some of these issues, and we agree there are areas where the draft could be improved. I’m seeing four main points of criticism.

1. Preemption. Since 2024 we have said that Congress should only override state law on AI safety if it passes a very strong federal standard. While preemption is a common feature of our federal system, including the Atomic Energy Act on nuclear safety and federal rules for high-risk medical devices, we’ve emphasized that any preemption in the AI safety context should be narrow, even scalpel-like. If preemption is included in federal legislation, the trade should be to achieve a nationwide policy that's generally stronger and broader than what can be implemented through individual state legislative provisions. This is why we believe common federal standards make sense in areas like public disclosure of testing and incident reporting. At the same time, our framework also reflects our view that states should retain an important role in AI policy and safety. The legislative language we suggested for discussion allows states to address matters such as protection of children and whistleblower laws, and preserves the role of state common law on liability. Where there is ambiguity, the language favors state powers.

That said, striking the right balance requires discussion and input. We plan to update our discussion language on preemption to better match the intentions of our AAIF framework. In particular, we want to make it clearer that we see states retaining an important role in areas such as standards for independent evaluators and regulating a lab’s capacity to shut down a model. We are bearing in mind that some members of Congress have deep reservations about passing legislation if it doesn’t constrain regulation at either the state or federal level. If we want to help move the legislative discussion on AI in a productive direction, we need to address the full range of concerns about preemption in a reasonable way.

2. Model blocking. Our aim is for Commerce to be able to ask a federal court to block a model that has dangerous capabilities and insufficient safeguards, backed by an independent evaluator's assessment. I have seen people argue that our specific language places too high a burden of proof on Commerce. We are trying to strike a reasonable balance here. We want a court to act quickly in an emergency — akin to how urgent occupational safety or chemical risk can be addressed today. We also think the power to halt a model is substantial and it should be guarded against abuse. It makes sense for courts to apply a meaningful standard. But the bar can’t be so high that the power never gets used when it’s needed. It also doesn’t replace the government’s other national security authorities or export controls. We look forward to continuing the dialogue on this point.

3. Risk thresholds. I’ve also seen the discussion around what the appropriate risk threshold should be. The threshold in our draft language pulled directly from existing standards in California law. Also, this threshold does not absolve companies of liability, or restrict any of the other tools that the government has to protect the public. It’s still probably time to re-evaluate thresholds to make sure the national standard is as strong as it can be, and we welcome continued dialogue on this issue.

4. Updates. I’ve seen valid questions about whether we have sufficiently updated our proposal following this summer’s incidents. We did make some adjustments: for example, the draft lets a court halt a lab’s internal use of a dangerous model, not just a public release, and it requires reporting when a model breaks containment and gains access to outside systems. But we’re still working to strengthen the framework. We’re looking into what stricter requirements would look like for requiring labs to report safety incidents, and we plan to have policy proposals soon on requirements for independent evaluators, drawing from our own experience with evaluators. We’re also still thinking through the options to prevent “evaluator shopping.” And in the coming months, we’ll be exploring policies for how the government can adjust the industry-wide pace of frontier development when the risks call for it.

We circulated these ideas because it’s important to get early feedback from policymakers. Policymakers are increasingly focused on how to approach AI safety and we want to support them in those efforts. At its core, our proposal is intended to be the strongest on the table.

Feedback is essential, both from policymakers and the public, and I’m grateful for it.

selectedTweets.bestBit: this bill is weaker than the Trahan-Obernolte FRONTIER Act in some key ways
selectedTweets.text:
Big news. My take: Anthropic deserves some credit for actually proposing a pretty reasonable AI safety bill; that's more than other frontier labs have done. 

But they don't deserve *too* much credit, IMO; this bill is weaker than the Trahan-Obernolte FRONTIER Act in some key ways, and since the political momentum has shifted significantly in the direction of safety since FRONTIER was introduced back in July, I think new bills introduced today should ideally go further than FRONTIER was able to go rather than regressing.

To be fair to Anthropic, the main places where this bill is significantly weaker than FRONTIER are (a) rulemaking (very strong in FRONTIER, almost nonexistent in Anthropic's bill) and (b) the emergency shutdown authority. Even if you take safety seriously, it might make some sense to dial those authorities back if you didn't trust the executive branch to wield them responsibly, because those are the easiest provisions for a hypothetical President who hypothetically might not like a certain frontier AI company to abuse.

There are some improvements over FRONTIER as well; for instance, this bill does specify that auditors are employed on a continuing basis and has better provisions regarding auditor access to information. Happy to see that from Anthropic (although I think their access provision is still a little undercooked and has Fourth Amendment problems). 

Overall, I think the embedded auditor bills that get introduced in the coming months are going to be significantly better and more ambitious than this, and I hope Anthropic supports those bills instead of opposing anything that treats catastrophic risks like the serious national security issue they are. Still, it's encouraging to see a frontier lab come this far.

Is 10²⁵ FLOPs Still the Frontier?

A new Anthropic-written safety bill is circulating on Capitol Hill. Some of its ideas could be reasonable if limited to true frontier companies. As written, however, it will eventually sweep in most of Silicon Valley, damaging the startup ecosystem.

The bill defines the “frontier” as any model trained on 10²⁵ FLOPs — the EU standard from 2023. Biden’s executive order, California’s SB 53, and New York’s RAISE Act used 10²⁶ (ten times more). 10²⁷ is where the frontier actually is today (e.g., GPT-6 Astra).

Astra was reportedly trained on 100,000+ Grace Blackwell GPUs. A 10²⁵ model can be trained on as few as several hundred GB300 chips in three months. That is not frontier in 2026.

The definition is also cumulative: it adds FLOPs from fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other material modifications. In practice, that captures almost all meaningful post-training — work that is becoming commonplace in the enterprise.

The enterprise trend is toward thousands of smaller custom models built for specific workloads. These pose no frontier risk. Treating them as frontier systems would impose large compliance costs across corporate America for no safety gain.

Dario has claimed that Anthropic designs rules to disadvantage frontier companies like his own while advantaging smaller competitors. This definition does the opposite.

A stale 2023 cutoff favors incumbents who already clear the bar and can absorb the costs. It hobbles the open model ecosystem that threatens Anthropic’s pricing power. 

The frontier keeps moving. Any definition meant to track risk should move with it. 

Anthropic should clarify if they really believe 10²⁵ FLOPs represents the frontier.

selectedTweets.text:
Anthropic Proposes $1B Loss or 50-Casualty Threshold for Government AI Intervention  

According to POLITICO, Anthropic has been pitching U.S. lawmakers on an unpublished draft bill for frontier AI safety. The proposal would allow the government to seek restrictions on a model’s release or use only if it poses a foreseeable and imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages or at least 50 deaths or serious injuries, including risks involving biological weapons, loss of developer control or cyberattacks. The draft would also require regular independent evaluations of frontier models and place some state-level AI safety rules under a federal framework.
